name: ChromeOS
summary: Commercial operating system developed by Google, derived from ChromiumOS and the Linux kernel, structured around the Chrome browser, immutable verified boot and isolated Linux and Android container subsystems.
license: Proprietary commercial (Google EULA) with upstream open-source ChromiumOS components (BSD licence)

content.introduction: ChromeOS is a commercial operating system developed by Google, initially launched in 2011 to equip Chromebook-type laptops. Designed around a web- and cloud-service-centred paradigm, the system favours simplicity of deployment, fast start-up, transparent updates without manual intervention, and strict partitioning of data and processes.
content.what_is_it: Technically, ChromeOS is derived from the open-source ChromiumOS project. Its environment rests on a specialised Linux distribution whose build chain and software recipes were adapted from Gentoo Linux (Portage package system and ebuilds). The system includes an official monolithic Linux kernel extended with vendor patches for power management and cgroup-based scheduling, topped by a simplified user space in which the Google Chrome browser acts as the desktop environment and main user interface.
content.verified_boot_and_immutable_storage: The ChromeOS security architecture is built around the Verified Boot technology coupled with a hardware security chip (Google Titan C or H1). A read-only portion of the firmware (Coreboot/depthcharge) establishes the hardware root of trust, verifying at each stage the cryptographic signature of the writable firmware, of the Linux kernel and of the security settings. The root partition (`rootfs`) is mounted strictly read-only and protected at block level by the dm-verity kernel driver. Updates run in the background without interruption through an A/B dual-partition system, with atomic switching at reboot and automatic return to the healthy partition in case of failure.
content.graphical_stack_and_user_experience: Unlike traditional Linux desktop distributions, ChromeOS does not include a standard X11 server in its native system layer. Display relies on the Freon stack, which talks directly to the Linux kernel DRM/KMS drivers for OpenGL ES and Vulkan hardware rendering. The visual environment is provided by the Aura window manager and the Ash shell (Aura Shell), while the built-in Wayland compositor (Exo) handles windowing and smooth composition of native applications, progressive web applications (PWAs) and graphical surfaces coming from virtualised environments.
content.virtualization_subsystems_crostini_and_a: To extend its capabilities beyond the web environment, ChromeOS includes a lightweight virtual machine monitor written in Rust called crosvm, running on top of the kernel KVM hypervisor. Through crosvm and strict Minijail sandboxes (seccomp, Linux namespaces), ChromeOS provides the Crostini subsystem (Termina virtual machine hosting LXD/Incus Linux containers under Debian) for developers, as well as the ARCVM subsystem (Android Runtime for Chrome in a VM) running the Android application ecosystem in complete isolation from the host system.
content.management_and_cloud_ecosystem: ChromeOS is optimised for centralised fleet management in enterprises and the education sector through the Google Workspace administrative console (Chrome Enterprise Upgrade). Administrators can apply hundreds of security policies, restrict the installation of extensions, manage kiosk modes and provision identities instantly. A variant called ChromeOS Flex makes it possible to convert old PCs and Macs into thin clients; it differs from ChromeOS devices by the absence of Google security chips and of verified boot, and by the unavailability of managed Google Play applications.
content.release_channels_and_cadence: ChromeOS offers three channels. The stable channel receives minor changes roughly every two to three weeks and major changes every four weeks; the beta channel is updated every week, with its major changes arriving about a month before the stable channel; the development channel receives one or two updates per week. Changing channel is reserved to the device owner and can be blocked on a device managed by an enterprise or an educational institution.
content.chromeos_flex_scope: ChromeOS Flex is officially supported only on certified models, chosen among mainstream PCs and Macs of the last ten years. Google documents two differences with ChromeOS devices: the security chips designed by Google and verified boot on the one hand, access to managed Google Play applications on the other. Fleet management requires a ChromeOS Enterprise or Education licence, and large-scale deployment can go through existing fleet management tools.
content.security_design_principles: The ChromiumOS design documentation sets out the security principles of the system: defence in depth, secure by default, least privilege and process partitioning. It also describes the corresponding mechanisms: sandboxing, verified boot and secure automatic update. ChromeOS, the commercial version, relies on this foundation; the security chips and verified boot are among the elements cited by Google as specific to ChromeOS devices compared with ChromeOS Flex.
content.documentation_and_resources: Three documentation sets coexist: the ChromiumOS design documentation on chromium.org for the architecture and security of the open-source foundation, chromeos.dev for developers (Linux environments, Android applications, web), and the Google help centre for release channels and user-facing features. The support pages specify the update cadences per channel.
content.origine_du_projet_et_lignee_googlebook: Google presents ChromeOS as a system available since 2011, maintained by automatic updates covering the system, the browser and the hardware at once. The administrator documentation places the current product line in a transition: a new family of devices, the Googlebooks, has been announced, and a page dated 23 September 2026 sets out what this announcement implies for existing fleets. It states that ChromeOS devices will continue to receive updates and security fixes until mid-2034, that ChromeOS Enterprise and Education licences already associated with devices are maintained, and that migration paths to Googlebook OS are planned for devices whose ten-year cycle extends beyond that deadline. The name of the system is therefore not separated from the hardware it equips: support dates are published per model and per hardware platform, not per software version alone.
content.update_duration_and_hardware_platform_li: The official policy sets the update period at ten years from the platform release date, a platform being the set of components that a manufacturer assembles for a given device. Google states that it works every two weeks with component manufacturers to test versions on each device, which ties the release cadence to hardware validation rather than to a release calendar. Dates are published per model in a table ranging from the earliest devices, an AC700 whose updates stopped in August 2016, to enterprise Chromebase units maintained until June 2028. For devices released before 2021, access to the full ten years requires an activation by the administrator, called extended updates; this activation does not preserve access to the Play Store or to Android applications, whereas devices released in 2021 or later receive these ten years automatically. After the last update, the system keeps its secure mode: at each boot it self-checks and restores its original state if it detects tampering.
content.linux_terminal_and_package_management: The base system is not administered through a package manager accessible to the user: system and browser components arrive through the automatic updates described by the support policy, and not through a package selection. A second software set is however documented separately. The Linux development environment, disabled by default, is enabled from Settings, About ChromeOS, Developers; its installation takes about ten minutes and opens a terminal on a Debian distribution, in which additional tools are installed with the APT package manager. The update command cited by the official help is `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get dist-upgrade`. Linux applications share a single sandbox: a harmful application can affect the other Linux applications, but not the rest of the system, and files shared with the Linux environment are accessible to all these applications. Access to this environment can be forbidden by the administrator on a managed device.
advantages: System initialisation and boot in a few seconds thanks to an optimised firmware and kernel sequence.
Security reinforced by design: immutable read-only root via dm-verity, Verified Boot and hardware security chip.
Fully silent updates with no session interruption through A/B redundant partitioning.
Versatile execution capabilities thanks to the isolated Crostini (Debian Linux) and ARCVM (Android applications) subsystems.
Highly centralised fleet and identity management through the Google Workspace administrative console for enterprise and education fleets.
Extended maintenance policy with up to 10 years of guaranteed security and feature updates on recent hardware.
disadvantages: Strong structural dependence on Google's commercial ecosystem and on connectivity to cloud services.
Proprietary operating system not freely modifiable without rebuilding the ChromiumOS project upstream.
No low-level administrator access in normal mode (developer mode disabling verified boot and erasing data).
Hardware compatibility restricted to configurations certified by Google (particularly for graphical acceleration under Crostini/ARCVM).
ChromeOS Flex does not support Android applications and requires standard x86-64 hardware.
who_is_it_for: Pupils, students and teachers working in educational environments managed by Google Workspace for Education.
Professionals, remote workers and enterprises looking for lightweight, secure workstations that are easy to administer remotely.
Users looking for a smooth web access terminal, requiring minimal system maintenance and immune to tampering with system files.
Web and cloud developers using native Linux development tools through the Crostini subsystem.
who_is_it_not_for: Users requiring a permanently offline workstation or refusing any synchronisation with an online commercial account.
Professionals depending on heavy native Windows or macOS software suites (advanced CAD/CAM, heavy professional multi-track audio and video editing).
Intensive PC gamers looking for full and direct support for DirectX libraries and specific simulation peripherals.
System administrators requiring direct granular control over the kernel and the host file system structure.
content.verdict: ChromeOS rests on a thin-client architecture, combining the Linux kernel, a cryptographically verified immutable read-only file system and virtualised environments under KVM (Crostini and ARCVM). It is designed for connected office work, education and standardised industrial deployments, and imposes in return a dependence on Google services as well as a strict separation between user space and the low-level components of the machine.
